title: Pip's Goblin Grudge
markdown:
The Whispering Crags kept hanging valleys and streams like silver leftovers, firs that bowed and sang whether anyone asked, a wind that wrote the same breezy song twice and called it tradition. Riven lived there with his feet on rock: the scent of pine needles after rain, the feel of a rough-hewn stone, the rustle of a rock ptarmigan changing its mind in the heather. Not a moonbeam elf. Mountain-bred, eyes always scanning the craggy slope as if the mountain might misplace something important.

His dearest companion was Pip, a mountain shrew, shadow and inconvenience in one small body. Pip could dart into a crevice no wider than a thumb and had a gift for choosing the worst possible cupboard — the one behind the kettle, the one that looked empty until it squeaked. Today he had outdone the gift. The cottage felt wrongly large.

“Pip. Scamp.” Riven’s call went out on the crisp air and came back empty. Boulders, mossy nooks — no shrew. Worry put a glint in the usual brightness. Pip was not only a pet. Pip was the habit of not being alone.

A dark sleek shape left the stream. Ink the otter, fur glistening with unasked-for mischief, shook a weather of droplets over everything. “Trouble?”

“Pip’s gone. And I have a goblin-y feeling.”

Ink’s whiskers worked. “They do take things. Pip is quick.”

“Too quick. The most impractical hide yet. And a certain trader.”

They took the shadowed ravine that looked spooky and was mostly junk: pots, rusty tools, stones with no career. Tucked in a less-travelled fold sat Gribble Grimfang’s stall, a scowl made flesh, eyes like trapped flies. In a wire cage of what looked like old knitting needles, Pip squeaked the language of insult.

Gribble squinted. “Lost something, elf? Or here for the slightly damp rocks?”

“Pip is mine. You took him.”

A wheeze of a laugh. “Found him stealing my polishing cloth. Return fee: a bag of sunstones and a perfectly preserved thunderclap.” A claw indicated the cage. “Escape artist. Nearly into the lint balls.”

Sunstones. A perfectly preserved thunderclap. A cold flutter started in Riven’s chest; his fingers tapped a worried rhythm on his leg. Those were not items you kicked up in scree. A goblin producing the exact wrong price at the exact right time had a cheekiness that almost counted as craft.

“I don’t have those.”

Ink’s cool fur against his trouser, a bright contrast to the ravine’s gloom. “Don’t worry — we’ll figure it. That wizard fellow? Professor Fizzwick? Grand ideas.” Cheerful as a dry pair of socks.

Fizzwick’s tower sat higher up, assembled as if by a flock of confused storks, perched on a rocky outcrop that had not been consulted. He was known for magnificent, slightly unreliable contraptions and a ladle that still believed soup should be an event. Riven and Ink scrambled the winding path, boots crunching loose stone, the stall’s scowl fading behind them and Pip’s last squeak travelling farther than was fair.

Inside: beakers, gears, scroll-avalanches waiting for a sneeze. The wizard himself, sprightly, beard a dandelion that had learned defiance, beamed. “Riven! Ink! The self-stirring ladle is still a tad enthusiastic. Innovation, you know.”

Riven told it straight. Fizzwick stroked gravity-defying white. “Gribble. Scoundrel. Fear not. I have just the thing.” From a pile that seemed to continue into the roof he drew a metal butterfly net married to a whirring fan, bendy handle, blinking lights. “Acoustic Repulsion Device. Frequency to discourage unpleasant noise. Neighbours. Possibly goblins.” Pride, uncontained.

Riven thanked him and did not inspect the theory too closely. They started back.

The caves came first: the sort that swallowed a word and spat it back twisted, as if the dark were practising impressions. Water ticked somewhere it could not be seen. Ink found a puddle worthy of a novel and splashed with both ends of himself. The enthusiastic echoes woke a colony of bats that had been minding their own leather business. They swooped; wings brushed Riven’s face like cold pages; the walls felt nearer; a low chitter filled the damp until he could taste it. He had no cage yet to clutch, only the picture of knitting-needle bars and a shrew with opinions.

They stumbled next into a meadow of cloud-sheep, woolly creatures floating just off the turf like naps that had learned to hover. They mistook Ink for a particularly buoyant patch of moss and lowered themselves to graze. Ink found this hilarious, wriggled free in a series of delighted squeaks, and exploded a weather of fluff that smelled of sunshine and dew. It tickled Riven’s nose. It clung to his sleeves as if hired. He used every mountain dodge he owned, ducking drifts that had ideas about his ears, while Fizzwick’s lights blinked in the net like an audience that did not understand the joke.

Gribble’s stall had gained a few more unhappy shoppers. Riven held up the device, lights cheerful as a lie. “A solution.”

Gribble sneered. “Fancy net. Price stands. These rocks will not admire themselves.”

“It will make the stall less appealing to noise.” Riven flicked the switch.

The machine did not repel. It produced the sneezes of a thousand mice through a megaphone. Riven’s hands found his ears. Ink vanished into a puddle. Gribble’s scowl became a grin, then a booming laugh.

“Not repulsion! My newest selling point! The Alarmingly Vocal Bargaining Aid! Imagine the racket!” He haggled with himself over a shiny goblin coin.

The noise drew trolls — burly, fond of volume — whose feet explained the ground to itself. They wanted the device. Gribble, scenting a better profit than an elf’s grief, shooed Riven off. Pip’s frantic squeak drowned. Riven felt a loose-stone dread. Flowers seemed to dim. He could not reach the cage through troll and greed.

He sat on a rock. Sun distant. “Too complicated. Pip trapped. Trolls. Gribble is a goat that learned barter.”

Ink’s wet nose, harder this time. “Figure something out. Pip is clever. He wouldn’t hide that well without an exit.”

Riven looked at the whirring net, the squeaks, the size of a shrew. What if Pip used the machine? What if the squeaks became his?

Professor Fizzwick arrived then in a giant teacup powered by flapping bellows, landed with a wobble, nearly donated the tea to the ravine. “A touch enthusiastic, I feared.” He took in goblin, trolls, upset shrew. “Classic. Improvement!” From a sleeve, a corked vial. “Sleep-inducer. A whiff. Works on grumpy goats. Trolls, I suspect, are cousins.”

Riven’s plan assembled itself from other people’s mistakes. “The device. The vial. Ink. Pip.”

He approached Gribble with the calm of someone selling weather. “This will make the stall quieter. Better for selling. No more squeak from my friend.”

Gribble’s scowl deepened. “Elf trickery?”

“Essence of quiet. A sigh. A nap.”

While the trolls argued volume, Riven eased the cork. Ink nosed a stone; puddle-water kissed the vial’s mouth; a fine mist found troll and goblin. Yawns. Booms became grumbles. Gribble’s eyes drooped toward a mumble.

Riven had not opened the cage door. He had angled the original squeaking fan at the gap. Pip, who understood gaps the way Fizzwick understood almost-inventions, wriggled out and into the machine’s heart. The shrew-amplified racket became tremendous. Half-asleep trolls startled with limbs like wet rope. Gribble, confused by noise and nap, tripped on a watering can.

Riven took the empty cage for later and the shrew for now. Ink diverted the remaining attention by sliding headfirst down a mud slope as if commissioned. They scrambled the rock path. Sleepy outrage faded behind.

Home smelled of pine and the particular relief of a door that knew them. Pip sat in Riven’s palm, grooming whiskers with paws too tidy for the day they had had, satisfaction too large for the body. Ink returned to his favourite stretch of stream and became a dark comma in the late sun. Professor Fizzwick perched on a rock as if it were a lectern and sketched a self-folding teacup that already buzzed with the threat of working. The bellows-cup, parked at a tilt, dripped mountain into the heather.

Riven stroked the small head. He did not lecture the firs about friendship, or about wizards with grand ideas, or about otter slides, though Ink would have seconded the slide. Pip bit his thumb, fondly, tasted salt, and began considering the cupboard behind the kettle as if the afternoon had been a rehearsal. The wind went through the firs as it always had. Down-valley, a troll snored like weather. The teacup on the rock folded once, unfolded, folded again, and looked guilty. Riven put the empty cage on a high shelf, where even a gifted shrew would need a committee to reach it, and put the kettle on for whoever was still awake enough for tea.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
